newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM maintains low profile at censure debate.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM maintains low profile at censure debate.

text.p: Key opposition leaders accused Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa of condoning corruption and mismanaging the economy as a long-awaited no-confidence debate against him started in parliament on Wednesday.
A grim Banharn listened impassively as opposition leader Chuan Leekpai of the Democrat Party and others launched blistering attacks on him.

"The prime minister is guilty of mismanaging the country, irresponsibility, lack of vision, turning a blind eye to corruption in his coalition and abusing power for personal gain," Chuan said in his address.
"From now on, the prime minister has lost the legitimacy to run the country as he will only bring damage to the nation and the democratic parliamentary system," he said.

At one point Banharn stood up and briefly denied opposition charges that he might have benefited from a recent government imposition of a surcharge on steel imports to assist the ailing local steel industry.
"A person I respect told me one day the steel industry would collapse soon if the government did not do anything. After investigations, I agreed that the industry needed help," he said.
"I did all that with sincerity. And I can tell you now I did not receive even one satang from the industry," he said.

Banharn was expected to give a more considered reply to the opposition accusations later this week. The televised debate on the opposition-launched no-confidence motion against Banharn was expected to last three days.
In their motion, the opposition accused the prime minister among other things of incompetence, economic mismanagement and plagiarism related to his master's thesis.

Banharn, whose six-party coalition has been in power for 14 months, has denied the accusations and vowed to defend himself in parliament. "I am 100 percent confident," he said on Tuesday when asked about his chances of surviving the debate.
His coalition controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament and political analysts expected Banharn to win the vote despite speculation that there might be cracks in his coalition.

Political analysts said big changes to government could come after this debate. Banharn could trigger a major cabinet reshuffle to appease critics and accommodate troublesome coalition partners or quit and hand over his post to another more acceptable politician in the coalition, they added.

Banharn's administration has been hurt by an economic slowdown, sluggish exports growth, a battered stock market that sank last week to near three-year-lows and a run on the baht by offshore investors after devaluation rumours.

He has also been plagued by political infighting within the coalition over cabinet posts and factionalism within his core Chart Thai Party. The local media has been hostile against him from the outset.

"The stock market has been battered during your government. We have said from the outset that the men you chose for your economic portfolios were not suitable for their jobs," opposition leader Chuan said.
Chatichai Choonhavan, who heads the Chart Pattana Party, the second largest opposition party, said Thailand was a leading regional economy in the past but not since Banharn took over.
"Our national debt has soared to US$80 billion and our future generations may not be able to repay," he added.
